title: SYNTHROID (levothyroxine sodium) tablets, for oral use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label set 1e11ad30-1041-4520-10b0-8f9d30d30fcc, version 1537, published 29 February 2024; initial US approval 2002
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, AbbVie Inc.
result: Boxed warning: thyroid hormones, including Synthroid, either alone or with other therapeutic agents, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss; in euthyroid patients, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction; larger doses may produce serious or even life-threatening manifestations of toxicity, particularly with sympathomimetic amines used for their anorectic effects. Contraindicated in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency. Warnings and precautions: narrow therapeutic index; overtreatment or undertreatment may have negative effects on growth and development, cardiovascular function, bone metabolism, reproductive function, cognitive function, gastrointestinal function and glucose and lipid metabolism; in children overtreatment is associated with craniosynostosis and acceleration of bone age. Over-treatment may increase heart rate, cardiac wall thickness and contractility and may precipitate angina or arrhythmias, particularly in patients with cardiovascular disease and elderly patients, who start at lower doses; arrhythmias are monitored during surgery in patients with coronary artery disease on suppressive therapy. Initiation before glucocorticoids may precipitate acute adrenal crisis in adrenal insufficiency, because thyroid hormone increases metabolic clearance of glucocorticoids. Addition of levothyroxine may worsen glycaemic control in diabetes. Over-replacement may increase bone resorption and decrease bone mineral density, particularly in post-menopausal women. Adverse reactions are primarily those of hyperthyroidism from overdosage, including arrhythmias, heart failure, angina, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, muscle weakness, decreased bone mineral density, impaired fertility; seizures reported rarely with institution of therapy; pseudotumor cerebri and slipped capital femoral epiphysis in pediatric patients; premature epiphyseal closure with compromised adult height; hypersensitivity reactions to inactive ingredients, including angioedema and serum sickness. Overdosage: confusion and disorientation; cerebral embolism, shock, coma and death have been reported; seizures occurred in a 3-year-old child ingesting 3.6 mg; symptoms may not appear until several days after ingestion. Interactions: increases the response to oral anticoagulants; may reduce the effect of digitalis glycosides; with tricyclic or tetracyclic antidepressants, increased risk of arrhythmias and central nervous system stimulation; with ketamine, marked hypertension and tachycardia; with sympathomimetics, risk of coronary insufficiency in coronary artery disease; phosphate binders including calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate, bile acid sequestrants, ion exchange resins, orlistat, proton pump inhibitors, sucralfate and antacids may reduce absorption; phenobarbital and rifampin accelerate metabolism; soybean flour, cottonseed meal, walnuts, dietary fibre and grapefruit juice may reduce absorption; biotin interferes with TSH, T4 and T3 immunoassays and is stopped at least 2 days before testing. Atrial fibrillation is the most common arrhythmia of levothyroxine overtreatment in the elderly. Long-term carcinogenicity, mutagenicity and animal fertility studies have not been performed.
